relation_definitions.knowledge_before: Incoming source was received/read before the target Darwin writing. A resolved target writing date supplies a conservative known-by bound, not an exact receipt day.
relation_definitions.replies_to: Source letter replies to target letter. This can point in either correspondence direction; only Darwin-authored replies with surviving incoming text can become Darwin response candidates.
relation_definitions.refers_to_own_letter: Source references another Darwin-authored letter or note. This records writing/document identity; it does not establish recipient receipt, a new incoming prompt, or availability of a later response to Darwin.
relation_definitions.receipt_without_reading: An incoming letter or unresolved reference was physically received but explicitly unread at the Darwin witness. This creates no knowledge availability or prompt eligibility.
relation_definitions.source_event_match: A source documents an event reported by Darwin, but his wording does not establish reading its whole text. Only the explicit event is attested; no incoming full-text availability or prompt is created.

policy_notes: Incoming text is never a target for learning Darwin’s voice, regardless of whether it has a reply.
A receipt acknowledgment alone does not establish a direct reply to that correspondent.

Catherine 287 remains available for 306, but the earlier case-study label acknowledged_received_and_responded_to is refined here: 306 is addressed to Susan. The earlier evidence snapshot is preserved.
Unlocated references remain graph nodes with null source text, never reconstructed conversation prompts.
Post-return review: a reference to an outgoing letter or dispatch plan is not proof of recipient receipt.
Incoming 323 corroborates the Herbert note history but has no established Darwin knowledge date; it must not be supplied as context to the earlier 314.
References with an unknown communication channel or uncertain addressee remain reviewed observations rather than invented incoming letters.

An identity/date screen is not a set of equally plausible antecedents: full-body reading and intervening shared contact, visits, or changed circumstances inform review without imposing a hard age cutoff.
Incoming full-read assessments, including historical-background matches, never activate knowledge dates or prompts by themselves; only separately accepted graph edges do.
coverage: All 288 audited catalogue candidates plus explicitly attested unlocated references. Relationships reviewed incrementally; absence of an edge is not absence of a historical relationship.

prior_temporal_observations.label: Year stated in the prose
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: Fanny Owen explicitly identifies the year in the body. This supports 1828 but does not independently establish the editorially supplied January date.

prior_temporal_observations.label: Return and discovery of waiting letters
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: Darwin links his return from the Welsh geological trip on 29 August to finding letters waiting. This is a dated event in the body, rather than the 6 September date of the outgoing letter. Individual documents still need matching.

prior_temporal_observations.label: Several dated writing sections
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: The letter contains writing on 8 February, 26 February, and 1 March 1832. Retain those sections; a single earliest date would place later observations too early.

prior_temporal_observations.label: Explicit receipt on a dated morning
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: The section dated 5 April 1832 identifies receipt that morning of Caroline's 31 December letter and Catherine's 4 February letter. The record as a whole spans 2–6 April, so 2 April cannot be the availability date for this batch.

evidence.anchor: I this morning received your letter of Decr 31 & Catherines of Feb 4th

prior_temporal_observations.label: Receipt day inside a broadly dated letter
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: Darwin gives 3 May as the day he received letters from Susan and Mr Owen, within a letter catalogued May–June 1832. The year comes from the letter context; the incoming documents still require matching.

evidence.anchor: Susans (& one from Mr Owen) I received May 3d

prior_temporal_observations.label: Impossible date retained as evidence
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: Catherine reports receiving a letter on 31 June, which is not a valid calendar date. Preserve the wording and flag it for review; do not choose a replacement day or month automatically.

prior_temporal_observations.label: Dated batches and a parcel without new letters
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: The 14 November 1832 section names letters from Catherine (25 July), Susan (15 August), and Erasmus (18th, month implicit). The 24 November section distinguishes arrival of a box from non-arrival of letters. Do not flatten all receipt evidence to the record's 24 October start.

evidence.anchor: Neither the Captain or myself have received

prior_temporal_observations.label: Continuation month corrected by an editor
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: A continuation is labelled March 8 in the transcription. Editorial footnote 9 identifies the month as an error for April. Retain the original March wording and the separate editorial correction; do not interpret it as an earlier receipt or writing event.

prior_temporal_observations.label: Separate May, June, and July knowledge states
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: The opening section dated 22 May 1833 acknowledges five letters dated September through January. A June section adds February and March letters plus notes. The 14 July section acknowledges Caroline's May letter and reports an April letter missing. Context available in July must not be supplied to the May section.

evidence.anchor: June:— I have just received a bundle more letters
the April one alas is lost

prior_temporal_observations.label: A correspondent disputes a missing-letter inference
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: Catherine explains that the April slot in their writing rotation may correspond to a letter dispatched at the end of March. This is evidence about naming and scheduling, not proof that Darwin had read her explanation before its own receipt is established.

evidence.anchor: I do not think there was any April Letter lost

prior_temporal_observations.label: Later section adds another received batch
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: The section dated 29 July 1834 acknowledges three family letters, the latest from Susan dated 12 February, plus books and notes. The letter began on 20 July; the later batch should not become context for the earlier section.

prior_temporal_observations.label: Long-delayed incoming letters and an unsent outgoing letter
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: In the opening section dated 24 July 1834, Darwin acknowledges Henslow letters dated 12 December and 15 January 1833 received together. On 28 October he explains that this outgoing letter has remained unsent since July; it continues into November. The catalogue's sent action describes a writing span here, not one proven posting day.

prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: In March 1835 Darwin reports receiving September and October letters while June–August letters remain missing. Receipt of a newer letter cannot activate every earlier letter in the catalogue.

evidence.anchor: The June, July, August ones have miscarried

prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: Darwin first reports recovery of three missing months, then three more letters in the continuation labelled July [August] 12th. Editorial footnote 1 explains the August correction. His stated completeness concerns this home-correspondence sequence, not every incoming correspondent.

evidence.anchor: I have received the three months letters which were missing

prior_temporal_observations.label: Explicit reversal of arrival order
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: Darwin explicitly says Fox's June and November 1834 letters reached him in reverse order. The outgoing letter is dated 9–12 August 1835; it does not supply the separate exact arrival days.

evidence.anchor: one dated June & the other November 1834

prior_temporal_observations.label: Receipt tied to a voyage event
prior_temporal_observations.interpretation: The December 1835 letter recalls receiving Caroline's March letter the day before final departure from the Galapagos. This separates the age of the received letter from the time of delivery and supplies a voyage-relative receipt constraint, without inventing a calendar day.

evidence.anchor: the day before finally leaving the Galapagos

prior_receipt_observations.scope: Correspondence and news from home; do not generalize mechanically to every correspondent.
prior_receipt_observations.evidence_anchor: the date of the last letter I received was 13 months ago
prior_receipt_observations.interpretation: The newest letter he mentions was itself dated about thirteen months earlier. This does not date its arrival or prove that no local letters reached him. Preserve the approximation; do not turn it into a precise global exclusion cutoff.

prior_receipt_observations.scope: Catherine's January letter received; older home correspondence still missing.
prior_receipt_observations.evidence_anchor: Nine months’ letters are wandering over the wide ocean
prior_receipt_observations.interpretation: Receipt of a newer letter does not establish receipt of all earlier letters. His expectation that the missing letters would arrive only after England is a contemporary prediction, not an actual receipt date.

prior_receipt_observations.interpretation: The missing-mail report extends beyond family correspondence, but a specific Henslow letter in the missing batch is conjectural.
